Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount. 


Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Cheers,
Marten

Driver also noted that someone had tried to upload a fraudulent bank statement.
** Driver notes that rider who called them during a specific trip and claimed to be from Bolt support. Driver gave up an OTP code to the scammer.
** Earlier that day, the following changes occurred on the account:
*** Email changed from [j752000@hotmail.co.uk|mailto:j752000@hotmail.co.uk] to [mrbolt0001@gmail.com|mailto:mrbolt0001@gmail.com]

** Reverted the email and phone number.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* This is clearly a case of UK phishing. Logged in the [tracker|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1ATgWnP67pDJIEwUJ5Wu0kqMuUWDhs-uw2TblAz0JQik/edit?gid=0#gid=0].
* We have already provided reports to the ICO. Since no financial detriment appears to have been suffered and the matter was resolved quickly, it is also not notifiable to the driver.

*Update*

* Read through available information 
* Identified some potential areas/ideas for updates/new info, but WiP (not set):

* *I. Choosing a Role (in-app)*
** *A.* Drivers can have multiple roles and switch between them.
*** *1.* CS needs to be prepared to assist drivers with registration for different roles.
*** *2.* CS needs to be able to guide drivers through the process of switching between roles in-app.
** *B.* Riders may see different categories based on the driver's selected role.
*** *1.* CS needs to be able to explain category availability to riders based on driver profiles.
*** *2.* CS needs to handle potential confusion from riders about changing categories.
** *C.* Data synchronization between driver profiles.
*** *1.* CS needs to be aware of which data is synchronized and which is not to answer driver questions.
* *II. Substitution*
** *A.* Drivers can delegate orders to other drivers (substitutes).
*** *1.* CS needs to be able to assist with the substitution enrollment process for both existing and new drivers.
*** *2.* CS needs to handle issues related to document verification for substitute drivers.
*** *3.* CS needs to address rider inquiries about orders being served by substitute drivers.
** *B.* Riders will see information about substitute drivers.
*** *1.* CS needs to be prepared to explain the substitution process to riders and the information they see.
* *III. Price Bid*
** *A.* Riders and drivers can negotiate ride prices.
*** *1.* CS needs to be able to handle disputes or questions regarding price negotiations.
*** *2.* CS needs to be aware of the limitations on price adjustments (+30%, -10%).
*** *3.* CS should be aware of dynamic pricing and how it affects price bidding.
*** *4.* CS needs to handle recalculations due to traffic or other delays.
*** *5.* CS needs to be aware of auto-acceptance features if implemented.
* *IV. Driver Requirements for Riders*
** *A.* Drivers can set requirements for riders.
*** *1.* CS needs to be able to explain driver requirements to riders.
*** *2.* CS needs to handle cancellations related to driver requirements.
*** *3.* CS must ensure driver requirements do not lead to discrimination.
* *V. Favourite Driver*
** *A.* Riders can favorite drivers.
*** *1.* CS needs to be able to explain the favorite driver feature to both riders and drivers.
*** *2.* CS needs to address any issues with the visualization of favorite driver status.

* On 8 April 2025, the following detail changes took place on the account of a UK driver ([profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/5616326?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]):
** Email changed from [hasantikman@gmail.com|mailto:hasantikman@gmail.com] to [mrblot002@gmail.com|mailto:mrblot002@gmail.com]
** Phone changed from +447300206201 to +447832429987
** Bank statements uploaded. After several attempts, it appears that on 12 April the bank details were changed:
*** account_iban changed from 08052763 to 00847210
*** account_swift changed from 777751 to 041368
*** payout_client_account_id changed from 20330896 to 22816809
* On 12 April 2025, driver called Bolt ([here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/554550287]), flagging that their details had been changed on their Bolt account, including changes to their bank details.
* Later that day, CS reverted the account detail changes as follows. As such, it appears that the incident is no longer ongoing:
** Phone changed from +447832429987 to +447300206201
** Email changed from [mrblot002@gmail.com|mailto:mrblot002@gmail.com] to [hasantikman@gmail.com|mailto:hasantikman@gmail.com]
** Bank details:
*** account_iban changed from 00847210 to 08052763
*** account_swift changed from 041368 to 777751
*** payout_client_account_id changed from 22818626 to 22819896
* It also appears that the driver has regained access to he account.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Given the email address bearing similarities to other UK phishing cases, we can be reasonably confident that this is a case of UK phishing. This is confirmed by order history (see e.g., [here|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/comms-channels/commsHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A%220%22%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22order_id%22%3A566325163%2C%22city_id%22%3A25%2C%22order_system%22%3A%22taxi%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] - lots of VOIP calls, likely that scammer asked for OTP details).

* Notifications:
** Already reported to the ICO, so can be considered as part of ‘ongoing’ incidents.
** Whether an A34 notification is needed depends on whether the driver suffered any actual financial detriment - TBC.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Confirm with CS: (i) was processed followed; and (ii) did the driver suffer any detriment. Once confirmed / A34 notification sent (if needed), this can be closed.

*Notification of a personal data breach*

We are writing to inform you about a recent incident.

*What happened?*

On 6 April 2025, we were made aware of an instance of phishing activity relating to your Bolt account. Individuals falsely holding themselves out to be members of the Bolt Support Team may have asked for information from you to gain access to your Bolt account. This may have resulted in temporary, unauthorised access to your account. However, we are not aware of anything that indicates that your information is at any further risk.

As this type of activity relies on tricking customers into providing account details, it can unfortunately still occur despite appropriate security measures. As such, we have outlined below some steps you can take to protect your account from this type of activity.

*What steps have we taken?*

Bolt is committed to addressing these incidents and has robust measures to prevent, limit, and mitigate unauthorised access to customer accounts. These measures include (but are not limited to) requiring authentication via a one-time password to access customer accounts from new devices when attempting to log into an account using a phone number. In addition, we mask rider and driver phone numbers on the Bolt app to preserve privacy and improve security.

As soon as we became aware of this incident, we immediately took action to ensure your account's security further and mitigate the potential for any adverse effects, including taking appropriate steps to ensure that any unauthorised third parties no longer have access to your account. We are continuing to take steps to enhance our security and to protect the information within our care.

*What is the potential impact?*

Our investigations indicate that some of your information may have been accessed as a result of phishing. *What should you do?*

As precautionary measures, we recommend that you remain vigilant regarding your personal information, including any financial accounts. Consider refreshing and avoid re-using online passwords. Be alert to any unusual requests for access to your data or credentials via email, in-app messages, telephone calls or any other means of communication - in particular, we suggest never sharing your phone number, email address and one-time verification codes with strangers.

One assumption that makes our estimates unbiased is that if we get the DGP correctly, errors are uncorrelated
We do not have access to errors (they are theoretical), but we have access to residuals that can direct us at problems:

So we plot autocorrelation plots to check how residuals are behaving. We find that our markets have residual correlation.

* just having correlation per se does not mean that models are completely off. 
* we can measure by how much off they are with simulations (already did in separate ticket)
* such correlation often would be opportunity for growth, suggesting additional things to take to account

* some markets might still have weekly seasonality (which is researched and handled in a separate ticket)

  Which is an indication of "small" "week-long" biases (see plot above)

Hello, [~accountid:5d95f00136d2520dde7ede17] and [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd].

According to the official explanation published by the State Data Protection Inspectorate, the right of law enforcement authorities to collect data, including personal data, is usually established in the legal act regulating the activities of a specific law enforcement authority, for example, the Law on Police of the Republic of Lithuania establishes the right of the police to request from legal entities and/or natural persons any data necessary for the implementation of police tasks, for example, to reveal or investigate criminal acts or administrative violations of the law, as well as the obligation of legal entities and/or natural persons to provide the requested information. In other words, the Law on Police of the Republic of Lithuania establishes the obligation for the data controller to comply with the Requests for the provision of data received. It is noteworthy that Article 6(1)(c) of the GDPR establishes that the processing of personal data is considered lawful when such data is necessary to process in order to “fulfill a legal obligation to which the data controller is subject”. Thus, in the case where the legal acts in force establish the obligation for the data controller to provide data to third parties, this obligation must be fulfilled. Otherwise, a legal or natural person may be subject to liability established in legal acts for failure to comply with lawful requirements of the police or other state institutions.

The above explanation does not in itself mean that we as the data controller having received a request from a law enforcement authority, are obliged to execute such a request without assessing the lawfulness and proportionality of such a request. The obligation to justify a request for the provision of personal data also applies to law enforcement authorities. Article 5(1)(b) of the GDPR provides that personal data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes (purpose limitation principle). Furthermore, point 31 of the GDPR preamble states that “Requests for disclosure by public authorities should always be made in writing, be reasoned and occasional and should not relate to the entire system of records or to the system of records”.

Given the above stated, when we receive requests from the police, we need to check them and if the request seems to be lawful we are obliged to provide the police with the requested information, including personal data.

Under this particular request, the police requests to get access to our data, including personal data. I would say that in general the draft response is well written, however I suggest adding an accent on the requested form for receiving the information, i.e. they ask to receive information about trips in real time, which means that they seek to get access to our systems. Due to this, we need to highlight that pursuant to the already specified GDPR requirements we are unable to provide information in this particular manner, however we are ready to provide the clearly specified and limited information, including personal data (if we have it in hand) in a written form. Also, we need to clearly answer to their question No. 2 concerning the possibility to redirect a suspicious orders to a specific driver so that police could control their actions following the applicable legal acts.

Also, in the said answer we need to refer not only to the conversation but to their initial letter as we need to respond to that letter and not a call. We can say that under this response we are responding to your request dated xxxx followed by the conversation on the phone on xxxx.

Because some recent changes where we target low demand periods have not had desired effects, my hypothesis is that the demand elasticity during such hours is weaker than the city average. I did some rough calculation on elasticity for the hours impacted by this proposal and that seems to be true. With -10% price change, elasticity data shows +9.7% rides, but after splitting, it seems that during the suggested hours the gain from same price drop would be +6% rides (+4.8% on weekdays only). So based on that I am rejecting this.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* We are seeing a spike in phishing cases in the Netherlands.
** Majority are drivers reporting attempts at account takeover. When driver is actually hacked, the case is escalated to Privacy.
** If scammer successfully takes over the driver’s account, we cannot fully trust the in-app messages (particularly requests to change bank details) that we receive from the ‘driver’ (despite KB saying that in-app messages are trusted).
* To deal with the trustworthiness of requests made over in-app messages, Tier 2 has been asking for selfie + ID to verify identity (CS cannot trigger formal verification, so this is the alternative). Once the ticket is resolved, the pictures are deleted. 
** As an alternative, Tier 2 could consider asking for a copy of a bank statement.
** Currently, no other alternative options have been proposed.
* CS wants to know if they can have this process confirmed by Privacy, or whether they should take an alternative approach.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] just wanted to sense-check your views on this given that it relates to selfie verification. IMO, {color:#36b37e}I think it is fine for CS to request a {color}{color:#36b37e}*_selfie_*{color}{color:#36b37e} in these circumstances{color} given that:
** We are aware of cases where scammers use in-app messaging to increase their chances of changing details on an account they have hacked. As such, it is worth introducing an extra layer of security in some form.
** It may not be effective to ask for confirmation of certain pieces of information (e.g., contact details / home address / etc.), as these may be visible on the account that the scammer has hacked already. Selfies would be a good alternative.
** We can argue this is already covered in the updated draft driver privacy notice.
** In certain countries (like the UK), driver selfie verification checks are _automatically_ triggered when certain incidents are raised (e.g., safety issues). This is not the same as phishing, but it is similar enough for this measure to be proportionate.
* However, in providing this advice, we should also flag that:
** We should not also ask for a copy of the driver licence / bank statement - this does not seem proportionate in the circumstances (particularly as we already have a driver licence copy on record), unless for whatever reason the selfie check is not working. 
** When the driver submits a selfie, we should check whether the selfie is identical to one the driver has previously uploaded / provided on a different CS ticket. This is because I saw a case last week where a scammer found a selfie in a previous CS ticket and used that the bypass the check.
** The selfie should be manually checked, not fed through an automated process.
** We should definitely delete the image when the ticket is resolved.
* Let me know what you think. If you agree, I will push this forward 🙂

This is a bit of a gray area, and you’re right that Bolt is a third party to the contract between the franchisor and franchisee. So, legally speaking — no, we are not entitled to see their private agreement. However, we are allowed to ask for it, especially since we're being asked to take specific action based on its terms (e.g., hiding profiles after the license ends).

The best approach is to make it clear that we're not demanding the full contract, but rather need it to validate the request in order to protect our platform from potential brand misuse. We don’t need the entire agreement — just the relevant sections.

For example, we could phrase the request like this:

_Since we're not a party to your agreement with the franchisee, we kindly ask that you provide just the relevant section of your agreement confirming the license end date and post-expiry brand usage terms. This helps us make sure we’re acting appropriately on our platform without stepping into internal business matters._

Hello, [~accountid:61374989bba6c7006a2616ba]. Apologies for a delay in providing my response. 


According to the EU Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83/EU), pre-ticked boxes for additional services—such as insurance, premium delivery, or gift wrapping—are explicitly prohibited. This is to ensure clear and informed consumer consent.


Such legal regulation is established under the the Article 22 of the Directive which states the following: _Before the consumer is bound by the contract or offer, the trader shall seek the express consent of the consumer to any extra payment in addition to the remuneration agreed upon for the trader’s main contractual obligation. If the trader has not obtained the consumer’s express consent but has inferred it by using default options which the consumer is required to reject in order to avoid the additional payment, the consumer shall be entitled to reimbursement of this payment._

In my view, the delivery services are deemed to be additional services regarding which, pursuant to the requirements of the Directive, consumer’s explicit consent is necessary.

Given this, if a business adds a service through a pre-ticked box, and the consumer doesn’t actively opt in, any resulting charge is considered unauthorized and may subject to refund as stated in the above mentioned Article 22 of the Directive.

As a side note, let me draw your attention that the discussed Directive is not a directly applicable legal act and therefore had to be transposed into national law in the Member States, including Estonia. This should have been done in 2013. 

Hope this helps, but if you have any further questions, please let me know. Thanks.

** _Immediate disclosure of the_ +_full registration number and name of the driver_+ _assigned to case 544701316, as Bolt’s system will retain the details of all assigned and cancelled journeys._
** _Confirmation that this incident has been escalated internally for investigation._
** _Notification that Edinburgh City Council will be contacted with this report as the licensing authority responsible for the driver._
* Unfortunately, CS has not dealt with this matter particularly well. As a result, it has escalated.
** CS previously said that we cannot share the driver’s data on data protection grounds. The rider responded “_I am not requesting the driver’s personal data_” - this is incorrect (i.e., they are). This includes vehicle registration number, provided that the driver is a private driver.
** Rider has slightly altered their response, and is now asking for the +_journey metadata_+ +of the trip+.
** CS recently advised the driver to report this issue through the police in order for us to release the info.
** On 1 April, the rider then asked for “+_A written explanation as to why Bolt believes a vehicle registration used in public commercial service is not disclosable_+ _to the complainant of a safety and discrimination incident—despite the journey being accepted and cancelled under traceable metadata_”.
* The rider is aggressive and not backing down - they send several messages back-to-back. However, despite saying 6 times that they will do so, they have not yet escalated the matter.
** Only escalated to Legal and Privacy yesterday (14 April).

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Driver name / registration:
** We do not ordinarily provide the driver’s name and vehicle registration number to riders, as (despite what the rider says) this is the driver’s personal data. 
*** [Driver|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/2695011?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] is a private driver. Name is Mohammad Arif, vehicle reg is RV69HNZ.
** However, Bolt can share data when in the legitimate interest of a third party (i.e., pursuing legal proceedings).
*** Rider has flagged “_Without this information, it is not possible to escalate the matter to Edinburgh City Council Licensing, who require the registration to process any investigation or licensing breach_”. 
** We should take a two pronged approach:
*** (a) Check to see if we have reported / will report it to the council. If we have / will, there is no need to share it with the driver. We can flag that the data is in fact the driver’s personal data, and that this has already been reported.
*** (b) If we have not / will not report it, and we are confident that there is no other means of the driver making the report, then since the data is limited we can share it based on Bolt’s legitimate interest.
* Trip metadata:
** We can provide this - it is [here|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/144kE6y_rzYhQxSGsd18KRXvEplTUnE8F].

Hey, [~accountid:5ccc34a5326cf40e4549d40d]. Thanks for the additional context!

It seems like we might need to more clearly define what _spam_ actually means within CS because right now, I’d say with 99% certainty that agents treat OoO messages, “thank you” replies, and messages unrelated to Bolt services as spam. I believe they even leave internal notes in Beehive, commenting that it’s a spam case.

That said, this doesn’t change the fact that the only correct way to handle those types of cases is to leave them *_untagged_*.

So I think the real question is—*should we now clearly distinguish that only non-actionable, irrelevant messages (like OoO replies or “thank you” notes) fall under the idea of "spam"?* Because promotional or marketing emails, while previously considered spam by both agents and your team as well (from what I gather), are no longer meant to be treated that way. With the introduction of the third-party user personas and the *Marketing proposal or advertisement* tag, those messages should now be properly categorised instead of being left untagged or labelled as spam.

It’s also worth noting that we have another KB article—🐝 [*Closing a case that doesn’t require agent's assistance*|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/4413476962578?country=global&language=en]—where agents are instructed on how to handle spam cases. This seems to reinforce that there’s currently a pretty broad (and inconsistent) understanding of what “spam” actually is across CS.

Unless you or [~accountid:5c8a411cf63c96739fd935a9] have a different view, I see two options moving forward:

# *Keep the articles as-is*, but reinforce through CS comms that:
#* We now have third-party personas and issue tags.
#* Marketing messages should be tagged accordingly and not treated as generic spam or left untagged.
# *Update the articles*, but only if we’re ready to clearly redefine what CS should consider spam (e.g., limit the term to irrelevant/no-action-needed messages only or whatever makes sense).

Happy to align on whichever direction makes the most sense! 🙏

Hi [~accountid:712020:61ca3c26-7f48-41c2-aa17-30a61b99b569] - I have had a quick look and my thoughts are as follows:

* The [+trip+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/1960539799/13?orderTryId=2365748960] that the rider has flagged took place from their [+account+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/1809861], which suggests it is *neither a case of: (a) phone number recycling* (indeed, the rider has confirmed that they still use the phone number on the account (ending in 0001))*; nor (b) another user’s account having this user’s emai*l.
* There are *no obvious signs of phishing on the account* (e.g., account detail changes, in-app comms, etc.).
* Based on the login history, the only device that was active on the account on 8 April (when the trip was taken - which must mean it was the device used to order the trip) was fkhdHjtbRu6_xj5Fi1-DcY, which was authenticated on the account in June 2021. This suggests that the device has been associated with the account for a while, which *suggests that it is not malicious* / owned by a hacker.
* On 8 April, all devices were logged out of the account. This suggests, at the very least, that *any incident is no longer ongoing*.

In terms of my best guess / next steps:

* We are not yet confident there has been a data breach here, as we don’t have enough information. I would ask the dev-user-auth-support channel for their opinion on what might have happened here.
* My guess would be the rider let someone use their account years ago from another device, and forgot that they had allowed them to do so. The person then accidentally took a trip on the account through the same device earlier this month.  However, this is just a guess.
* Once we have more visibility on what caused this, and if we confirm that unauthorised access did occur here, then this should be reported to the ODPO team. It is very unlikely that this will be notifiable to the regulator / affected users.
* Be mindful there also may be a DSAR element here (for the device details - see the Beehive thread) - please look into this 🙂

* Instead, given that User A’s email address was present on Account 1 until 13 April 2025, User A would have received email notifications about the trips that User B took or tried to take through Account 1. This is what brought the incident to User A’s attention. As such, there are two data breaches that have taken place here:
** *User A’s data*: User B has access to User A’s account (Account 1), and so has access to any of User A’s data still on the account.
** *User B’s data*: User A has been receiving notifications about User B’s trips  attempted trips. We need to understand what information about User B was contained in those notifications.

The payments with the expired card were successful due to a feature not a bug. This can sometimes cause confusion among customers.

Mastercard's Automatic Billing Updater (ABU) are services designed to automatically update cardholder information for merchants, ensuring uninterrupted recurring payments and reducing transaction declines due to outdated card details.​
Customers card has a token and when they attempt to use their expired card then Bolt automatically checks with the customers bank. If they have a new card issued to with the same token then we are able to allow the payment through the expired card.

*EU Battery Regulation – Summary of Battery Associates Advice (April 2025) -* _Internal Analysis_

----

h3. 1. *Temporary Import for Repair – Registration Requirements*

*Question:*
If a battery is temporarily imported into another Member State for repair and not placed on the market (e.g. PT → PL), is registration required? Can it be returned to the original country?

*Battery Associates Summary:*

* No registration required in the second country if the battery is not being placed on the market.
* Shipment must still comply with *Annex XIV* documentation requirements (e.g. testing records, transport documents).
* If the battery is *substantially modified* (e.g. repurposing or remanufacturing), it is considered newly placed on the market and must be re-registered in the original country.

*Implication for Bolt:*
We can repair across borders without triggering new producer registration, but must maintain compliance with used battery shipment rules under Annex XIV. Legal/ops need clear definitions of what constitutes "repair" vs. "repurposing" to avoid accidental non-compliance. Recommend updating compliance SOPs for cross-border repair logistics so it’s defendable if we attract regulator scrutiny.

----

h3. 2. *Waste vs. Damaged Battery – Harmonisation Across the EU*

*Question:*
When does a battery become “waste”? Is this definition harmonised? Will Annex XIV help clarify?

*Battery Associates Summary:*

* "Waste" is harmonised at EU level via Directive 2008/98/EC: a battery becomes waste when it is discarded or intended to be discarded.
* “Damaged” is not a defined legal term under EU law.
* Annex XIV deals only with transport documentation for used vs. waste batteries and will not address or harmonise the “damaged” status.

*Implication for Bolt:*
We can rely on a consistent EU-level definition of waste, but must define “damaged” internally (e.g. via SoH thresholds or risk profiles) to support operational classification and compliance decisions. Recommend creating an internal decision tree to route batteries based on condition.

----

h3. 3. *Annex XIV Testing Exemptions – Diagnosis Shipments*

*Question:*
If we're sending batteries for diagnosis under Annex XIV §2b/c, can we skip the testing and recording requirements in §3?

*Battery Associates Summary:*
Yes – if the shipment is under a valid B2B agreement and for purposes of warranty repair, refurbishment, or root cause analysis, the requirements in §1a, §1b and §3 (including SoH testing) do not apply.

*Implication for Bolt:*
We can reduce regulatory burden for diagnostic shipments, provided we maintain the correct paperwork. Contracts and transport documents should explicitly state the diagnostic purpose under §2b or §2c. Recommend standardising declaration templates for recurring logistics partners.

----

h3. 4. *Cross-Border Registration – Country-by-Country Obligations*

*Question:*
Do we need to register every time batteries cross into a new market? (e.g. PL, PT, EE, DE)

*Battery Associates Summary:*
Yes – registration is required in *each Member State* where Bolt places batteries on the market for the first time. This applies to both new and reused batteries. Partnerships with recycling organisations do not eliminate the obligation unless they act as formal authorised representatives.

*Implication for Bolt:*
We must track first market placement and ensure registration is completed per country. Recommend developing a central registry or tracking system that links battery IDs with country of placement and registration status. Validate that recycling partners are legally empowered to act as authorised reps.

----

h3. 5. *Post-Sale Waste Responsibility*

*Question:*
If we sell a battery to a third party, do we remain responsible for its end-of-life handling?

*Battery Associates Summary:*
Not addressed in the Battery Associates report. However, under EPR principles, the responsibility generally remains with the party that first placed the battery on the market unless explicitly transferred by contract and recognised under local law.

*Implication for Bolt:*
We likely retain liability unless the buyer is registered and accepts EPR obligations. In B2B sales, contracts should shift waste management obligations to the buyer where feasible. Legal follow-up required in key markets.

----

h3. 6. *Need for Internal Battery Registry*

*Question:*
Do we need to maintain an internal registry of batteries and their country of placement?

*Battery Associates Summary:*
Not directly addressed, but each Member State requires separate producer registration, and there is no EU-wide registry.

*Implication for Bolt:*
*Yes – operational necessity*. We should build or integrate a tracking mechanism (linked to FleetOps or inventory systems) to log battery serials, country of import, and registration status. This will be critical to demonstrate compliance and avoid missed obligations as batteries move cross-border.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*IN SUMMARY*

* Please confirm the following:
** What *_personal data_* will Bolt be sharing with Odysse (or vice-versa), and *_why_*?
** In what *_direction_* is any personal data being shared?
** Will Odysse be able to use the personal data being shared *_for its own purposes_*?
* Subject to the above, if we are sharing personal data with Odysse, we should:
** (i) Be clear on the precise reasons *_why_* we are sharing this data;
** (ii) Ensure we are only sharing what is *_strictly necessary_*; and 
** (iii) Ensure a *_data sharing agreement_* is in place (which I can prepare).
{panel}

Further details / context is below.

*What personal data are we sharing?*

We (i.e., Privacy Team) are only concerned about any [+personal data+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3714777447/What+is+personal+data] that we may share with Odysse. Applying this to the categories you have listed:
* *Hotspots across the city*: Would these just be areas of a city (e.g., Brixton is busy at 2pm), or would this be linked to specific drivers (e.g., Driver X is usually in Brixton at 2pm)? If the former, it is unlikely to be personal data, and so from a Privacy POV we would have no concerns with sharing this.
* *Bolt average metrics*: Would this data all be aggregated (e.g., the average acceptance rate of Bolt drivers in London is 75%) or not (e.g., the acceptance rate of Driver X is usually 75% or higher)? If the former, it is unlikely to be personal data, and so from a Privacy POV we would have no concerns with sharing this.
* *Odysse performance metrics*: Can you provide more details on what this is? If it is information that cannot be linked to specific individuals in any way, then it it is unlikely to be personal data.
* *Details about safety blocks*: Again, can you provide more context here? Is this general information on the safety blocks that Bolt applies (e.g., Bolt may block a driver for harassment of passengers), or details of a safety block applied to a specific driver (e.g., on 10 March 2025, Driver X was blocked because they allegedly harassed a passenger). Only the latter would comprise personal data.
I therefore need further context on the above before I can fully advise. If we are not sharing any personal data, then there is nothing to advise from the Privacy side.

*Purposes and proportionality*

If we are sharing personal data here, we need to be clear on exactly why we need to share it. This is both so that: (i) we can be confident that the data sharing is proportionate; and (ii) I can be confident that this is covered in our driver privacy notice (which breaks down processing activities according the _purpose_ of processing).
Please therefore confirm why we need to share each datapoint (insofar as it is personal data) with Odysse. If any of the data sharing is superfluous / not strictly necessary, my advice would be to strip it back.
In particular, it would be helpful to know more about sharing details of safety incidents with Odysse - what are we sharing here, and why does Odysse need it? This information is sensitive, and so we need to be extra careful here. If Odysse is acting as a fleet, how much of this information would they already be able to access via the Bolt Fleet Portal? 

*Data sharing agreement*

When sharing personal data with a third party, we should make sure we have a data sharing agreement in place to ensure that: (i) we are taking appropriate steps to keep driver data secure; and (ii) Bolt is contractually protected if Odysse does anything with the data that causes drivers to be concerned. I can prepare a draft if needed, which can be done relatively quickly.
However, before preparing the draft, I need to understand the following:
* The specific personal data that is being shared here, as well as the purposes of sharing (see above).
* Which direction the data is being shared (i.e., is Bolt just sending personal data to Odysse, or does it go both ways?).
* If Bolt is sharing personal data with Odysse, will Odysse be able to use this information for its own purposes, or will Bolt restrict what Odysse is able to do with the data?

CS logged User out of all devices and instructed User to log back in → here the CS did not follow the process quite well. CS is first supposed to confirm that phone number is up to date. Then they should log out user out of all devices linked and User will log back in with their legit device, all other devices will be deactivated. If the former (i.e., dashcam), then this is not something we have much control over - indeed, in order to sidestep a lot of data privacy law issues, our position is that it is the driver that is the controller of dashcam recordings, and so we need to be careful not to exercise any control over how the driver uses their dashcam. All we should do in such circumstances is the following:

* Write to the driver and remind them to comply with data privacy obligations when using a dashcam (e.g., “_We have received a message from a passenger who is concerned about recordings made via a dashcam in your vehicle. While we do not control what you record on your dashcam, we kindly request you to take into account that laws protecting personal data, including the EU GDPR, apply to you when you process, use, collect and share personal data.”)._
* Write to the passenger to say that we have reached out to the driver to remind them of their data protection obligations.

If the latter (i.e., recording without their knowledge), please check with the local [+GFT Team+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3600842870/Global+Field+Team] whether this is a violation of any of our Driver Terms & Conditions. * Second master switch ( co-master ) setup was successful

!image-20250417-110848.png|width=66.66666666666666%,alt="image-20250417-110848.png"!

* Reason

The primary cause of the co-master setup failure was a data collation between MySQL versions. 

MySQL 5.7 uses {{utf8mb4_general_ci}} as the default collation, while MySQL 8.0 defaults to {{utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci}}. 

When MySQL 5.7 acts as the master, a MySQL 8.0 replica accepts data written in {{utf8mb4_general_ci}} without issues. 

However, if MySQL 8.0 becomes the master and commits data using its default collation ({{utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci}}), MySQL 5.7 replica cannot interpret this collation, resulting in replication failure.

To maintain replication compatibility between MySQL 5.7 and 8.0, all data written to MySQL 8.0 must explicitly use the {{utf8mb4_general_ci}} collation.

The current implementation of listFilesPaginated doesn't provide the same comprehensive file listing as listFiles. When using listFilesPaginated with a prefix (e.g., "documents/"), files in subdirectories (e.g., "documents/notes/file.txt") are rolled up into CommonPrefixes entries rather than being individually returned. This requires multiple subsequent requests to fully traverse the directory structure, which is inefficient for applications needing a complete file listing. We should modify listFilesPaginated to offer an option to disable the delimiter behavior, allowing it to return a flat list of all files similar to listFiles while still maintaining pagination capabilities.

Example:
If you have the following files in S3:


{noformat}documents/report.pdf
documents/spreadsheet.xlsx
documents/notes/meeting1.txt
documents/notes/meeting2.txt{noformat}

Using listFiles with prefix "documents/"

Will return a flat list of all 4 files:


{noformat}documents/report.pdf
documents/spreadsheet.xlsx
documents/notes/meeting1.txt
documents/notes/meeting2.txt{noformat}

Using listFilesPaginated with prefix "documents/"

Will return:

Currently AIoT is protected from almost all remote attacks by virtue of not talking directly to Internet (IoT forwards and spoonfeeds all of its communication).

This will change if IoT has direct access to Internet:

* If IoT shares its Internet access using NAT, AIoT is still protected from incoming traffic. But it will make outgoing connections which can be eavesdropped, redirected, forged, malicious, etc.
* If AIoT gets a GSM modem connected directly, it _can_ receive a public IP and unfiltered incoming traffic from Internet. In this case we need to additionally make sure that incoming connections are blocked by a firewall, services are up to date, etc.

h1. +LEGAL BASIS FOR TRANSFERS+

* {color:#4c9aff}Most kinds of data{color} = *Legitimate interest*.
** See [+LIA+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qVOFi8q4g2k-ItqYwB8igkV4EURkBedieXbBT1LYhXs/edit?tab=t.0].
* {color:#4c9aff}Biometric data{color} = *Legitimate interest* + {color:#ff5630}Substantial public interest.{color}
** I have chased on this [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08HT2MDFL3/p1742817559215399?thread_ts=1741972564.349499&cid=C08HT2MDFL3]. See also [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08PAF5UBJM/p1746010988779959]. However, no stakeholder (neither Ops, nor Safety, nor Product, nor Eng, nor Legal) has been able to confirm this point - it seems that nobody knows. As such, it is unfortunately left to Privacy to find a way to cater for this without full visibility of the facts.
** Taking a common-sense approach, it is _possible_ (albeit unlikely) that we may need to share biometric data between the entities (e.g., let’s say Bolt Ops OU stores the data on Admin, and the UK police then reach out to a local UK entity asking for biometric data for use in a criminal investigation - in such circumstances, data sharing of biometric data would need to take place).
** The preference would be not to share this data. However, if we had to share biometric data we cannot reasonably rely on consent - As such, we would need to rely on *substantial public interest* (i.e., preventing and detecting unlawful acts).
** We therefore have two options: (a) Do not include biometric data in the DSA, and advise the business not to share; or (b) Include biometric data in the DSA, and rely on substantial public interest if challenged. TBC with the Privacy Team.
* {color:#4c9aff}Criminal background data (drivers){color} = N/A
** This checked by the council.
* {color:#4c9aff}Fraud / criminal investigations{color} = Primarily *legitimate interest*, but if needed Paragraphs 10-12 of Part 2 of Schedule 1 of the DPA 2018.
** If we did need an alternative legal basis here, it would be:
*** The +prevention or detection of unlawful acts+ under Schedule 1, Part 2, Paragraph 10 of the Data Protection Act 2018;
*** Protecting the public against dishonesty under Schedule 1, Part 2, Paragraph 11 of the Data Protection Act 2018;
*** Complying with regulatory requirements relating to unlawful acts and dishonesty under Schedule 1, Part 2, Paragraph 12 of the Data Protection Act 2018; and/or
*** Exercising and defending legal claims under Schedule 1, Part 3, Paragraph 33 of the Data Protection Act 2018.
** Based on research, it is arguable that fraud  criminal activity data does not yet fall under A10 UK GDPR if it is merely suspicion / a contractual matter (i.e., fraudulent activity being used as a basis for suspending a user in accordance with Bolt’s T&Cs).
*** It would only definitely cross this threshold if it were formally legally assessed as a crime / reported to the police / treated as a criminal matter.
** Conclusion: Bolt can primarily rely on *legitimate interest* here. In order to ensure that we are not shooting ourselves in the foot in terms of documented position, we will assume for the purposes of the LIA that we are not processing any Article 10 UK GDPR data here.
*** If we were to share any Article 10 data, we can rely in Schedule 1, Part 2, Paragraphs 10-12 in order to do so. No need to document this for now - but we should keep it in the back pocket.

Initial objective was to merge all {{reinitializeS3Bucket()}} implementations into a single one in {{bolt-server}}, but there’s also the newer {{InputS3}} in NJSC. Scope extended to fix the bug in NJSC and modify all tests to use the NJSC version.

My plan is to handle this in several steps:

# Remove all duplicates from {{bolt-server}} and consolidate under one clean version (the one I added in this PR based on the Geo original)
# Fix the bug in the NJSC version: [InputS3|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-nodejs-common/blob/develop/src/componentTests/input/InputS3.ts]
# Attempt to migrate all tests in {{bolt-server}} to the new NJSC s3 utils semantics. Will only do where it's trivial and doesn't require understanding the test logic, in those cases the product teams will handle it on their own.

Our ideal objective is to have only the NJSC InputS3 version because it supports configless, but it's ok if _some_ tests in {{bolt-server}} will still use the one version that I just added in this PR. Even in an sub-optimal case we would still (1) fix the bug in all implementations and (2) remove needless code duplication.

“Following this previous ticket [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/CCM-19813|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/CCM-19813|smart-link] , I'm raising this ticket in order to request the revoke of the requirement to request the mention of Legal Basis in any request for information from any Police authority in Portugal.

The legal basis of this request is the following:

In Portugal, all Police forces (Judicial Police, PSP, GNR) are classified, under Law 49/2008, of August 27, as criminal police forces, with competence under this Law for the investigation of crimes and the request of information, at their own initiative, in any situation investigating the possible commitment of a crime, following a complaint presented or under the discretionary power Police forces have to investigate any situation they came across in the execution of their functions.

Also, under Directive n.º 1/2002, of April 4, the Public Prosecutor automatically delegates its competence in the Police forces mentioned above to carry on any actions in their name, in criminal processes that are strictly of their competence.

Therefore, either at their own initiative or when obeying a request from the Public Prosecutor, the Police forces always have legal basis to direct information requests to companies or citizens and they don't need to quote the legal basis for each individual request since this is a legal capability directly emerging from applicable law, and any request can be directly answered.”

25W16: Summary: Salesforce (SF) dependency is currently a blocker for centralizing control on our part. After analysis, we’ve discovered that on average there is an update every 2 days for the providers managed through SF (ROD). As such, we agreed the complexity implied is not worth this dependency and update support will be removed ASAP by SF team. We’ll support SF pricing config only on creation for ROD providers, and use Provider service as a proxy due to complex and hard to maintain OAuth integration with SF done on their level. 

*Detailed status:*

* After collecting data from Presto, I analysed all provider pricing updates made via Salesforce between 29.05.2024 and 16.04.2025. Key findings:
** 196 valid updates were recorded, with an average of 16 updates per month.
** When accounting for multiple updates to the same provider on the same day, the number reduces to 177 distinct updates.
* Key issue identified:
**  There were 34 updates where the surcharge_distance_ranges object was removed during the update process.
*** 28 of these occurred in April 2025.
*** This behaviour can lead to incorrect pricing configurations for providers.
* As a result, we raised a critical concern:
** We recommended that provider pricing updates via Salesforce be disabled as soon as possible to avoid further risk.
** The Salesforce team has acknowledged the issue and begun implementing the required code changes.
* Switch to delivery-pricing-eater as source for provider-level data
** finished updating test suite to align with new data model version
* Add support for storing pricing overrides when creating a ROD provider from Salesforce
** started implementing [+agreed solution+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05RK5Y3HQR/p1744715473799389?thread_ts=1743581575.765589&cid=C05RK5Y3HQR] with Salesforce team
** FYI we will only support storing Provider overrides of Eater fees for creation of Own delivery providers from Salesforce
** will make use of provider integration with Salesforce to avoid adding 3rd party authentication to our service

25W16: 1.Started working on creating a job ID (session key identifying a new courier order queue lifecycle) required for A/B testing effort based pricing; 2. Started computing high Last Mile Delivery (LMD) feature - providers whose LMD exceeds p80 of providers over the last 90 days. 

*Detailed status:*

* *Done* - Create new tables to store delivery job IDs
** {{delivery_job}} - stores job and courier IDs
** {{delivery_job_order_courier}} - stores the relationship between {{order_courier_id}} and {{delivery_job_id}}
** Added {{delivery_job_id}} as a foreign key for proposals.
** All schema changes are merged and deployed
* *In progress* - Assign delivery job IDs to courier earning proposals
** Logic is done, need to write tests
** For the moment, we won’t be enriching proposals responses with job IDs. The job ID will only serve targeting and analytics purposes.
* *In progress* - Design a profiling query to compute a list of providers with high LMD
** I wrote the query but now I need to integrate it into profiling and make sure it’s available on the backend. Will check with Laura to see if the query is correct
** The query identifies providers with higher than average LMD if their average LMD over the past 90 days exceeds p80 of city-level average LMD

According to the contract (9.5 clause thereof), Bolt shall have a right to terminate the contract at convenience by providing the Contractor with 30 calendar days notice (please note that no 3 months period is applicable). The mentioned notice addressed to the contractor would be quite a straightforward document. This definitely would be the safest and the most recommended way from a legal perspective to terminate the contract.

Pursuant to the clause 9.8 (e) of the contract, Bolt shall have a right to terminate the contract immediately if upon sole decision of Bolt the Contractor fails to perform the services in accordance with the terms of the contract. Given this clause, it seems that we have an opportunity to terminate the contract by providing the contractor with a written termination notice of an immediate effect. However, this termination notice shall, amongst other things, contain a solid ground for stating that the Contractor failed to provide the services as it is explicitly required under the contract. To this end I think that it would good mentioning about the Contractor not meeting the established SLAs and KPIs of Bolt. For that I would need very specific details how those SLAs and KPIs have not been met by the Contractor (stating that task completion rates have been consistently below expectations is not sufficient).

If it is agreed to proceed with the termination option available under Clause 9.8(e) of the contract, I must emphasize that this course of action carries a significant risk of triggering a dispute between the Parties

Please let me know how we shall proceed further.

Thanks.

Hey, [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] - 

*Background:* Several months ago, we concluded a DSA with a company that owns a tool for digital car inspections. They came back to us with an information that in fact, we will also be collecting personal data of vehicle owners, not only of the drivers. We prepared an Addendum that is still to be sent, however, would you like to advise me on certain aspects of this Partnership?

*Vehicle Owner Data*

*I. Through the CarScan App*

Firstly, the data is collected directly from the drivers by CarScan. Data of VOs is name, surname and phone number. They generate a report that we subsequently receive. We do not collect nor verify this data - we simply receive the reports.

*II. Creation of a database*

Business wants to gather the owner's info to build our car owner database to identify potentially unregistered fleets. Therefore, it intends to bulk download reports, extract VOs information and where that info is missing, to use some third-parties to identify/ look up the missing owner data from government sources (using VIN - the windshield number). With that information, allegedly, we would be able to approach individuals, whose multiple cars (unregistered fleets) operate on our platform and then engage with them directly to propose partnerships with clear benefits.

*III. Questions*

*A) The data collection question*

Vehicle owner data is collected by CarScan from drivers, who are often not the owners. To ensure adherence to POPIA (which is not substantially different from other high-standard legislation, I recommend:

a. Prepare an authorisation form for the drivers in relationship with CarScan that confirms that they provide accurate information and have been authorised to share such information;
b. If feasible, CarScan should notify owners via SMS that their data has been submitted.

OR

c. In the DSA, we explicitly state that CarScan confirms that the data about Vehicle Owners that they provide to us in reports is accurate/ up-to-date, etc. Bear in mind that in such cases, we cannot have the 100% certainty, thus the original plan to identify the unregistered fleet-owners may be ineffective.

*B) Database Question*

Using the data to build a *car owner database* goes beyond the original inspection purpose. Under POPIA (Section 18), owners must be *informed* of this new use. Key questions:

* Should the *DSA addendum* clearly state that *CarScan is responsible* for lawful collection and owner notification?
* Is it our responsibility to notify the Vehicle Owners? Or even if data is lawfully collected, do we need a way to *inform owners* about this new use ourselves?

Looking forward to hearing your thoughts!

*Things to note in the Figma designs:*

* DRIVERS:
** During the registration flow, drivers select their working profile. Under this, there is a disclaimer in which the driver accepts the privacy policy.
*** {color:#ff5630}*Should be privacy* {color}{color:#ff5630}+*_notice_*+{color}, and go to the right link.
*** Users cannot ‘accept’ a privacy notice. Instead, they should {color:#ff5630}*acknowledge it*{color}.
*** -Technically, the user is not yet a driver, and so the driver privacy notice does not yet apply. We should- {color:#ff5630}*-consider including disclaimer language-*{color} -to address this. We should also- {color:#ff5630}*-consider what data we have collected before the account is created-*{color}-.-
**** -_Bolt collects information on the working profile under which you choose to register to ensure that you are directed to the correct registration flow. Bolt processes such information based on contractual necessity in accordance with Article 6(1)(b) of the UK GDPR. For further information on how Bolt processes personal data, please refer to our privacy notice._-
** Acceptance Rate and Average Rating provided to driver in each profile.
*** Sidebar shows Driver Score to driver - {color:#ff5630}*should it*{color}?
** Drivers can switch profiles only when they are offline.
*** If this is the case, we are presumably not tracking their location. {color:#ff5630}*How can we ensure the driver only uses the agency model in the RoUK*{color}?
** To add an agency model profile to a principal model account that already exists, it appears that the driver just needs to click ‘Activate’ and it is done. This suggests all relevant data will be synchronised, and the driver is not inputting any information during the process.
*** By the same logic, it looks like the driver won’t have to re-complete verification.
* RIDERS:
** Fare card shows a breakdown of the fare, and a brief note that final prices may change.
*** Worth considering {color:#ff5630}*how much information we can provide about price setting*{color}, due to ICO investigation.

This concern is also relevant in the Canadian context, where courts consider the degree of economic integration between drivers and a platform. Even if a driver is not contractually bound to work exclusively for one platform, courts may still find economic dependence if the driver relies primarily on that income. If Hopp were to implement incentives that encourage platform loyalty, it could further strengthen the perception of dependency and increase the risk of drivers being classified as employees.

Hi, as today is a public holiday in the UK I am unable to verify this for you externally. I am not familiar with this project nor the specific UK procurement rules. 

The guidance for PPN 06/21 does not explicitly state that emissions data from parent or group entities must be included when the bidding entity is a subsidiary or shell company. However, it provides provisions for such scenarios.​

_According to the PPN 06/21: Frequently Asked Questions, if the bidding entity is part of a group and lacks separate emissions data, it may submit a Carbon Reduction Plan (CRP) covering both itself and its parent company, provided certain conditions are met:​_

* _The bidding entity is wholly owned by the parent._ 
* _The parent company's CRP includes a commitment to achieving Net Zero by 2050 for UK operations, which is supported and adopted by the bidding entity._
* _The environmental measures outlined in the CRP are applicable to the bidding entity during contract performance._
* _The CRP is published on the bidding entity’s website.​_[_GOV.UK+2GOV.UK+2GOV.UK Assets+2_|https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/procurement-policy-note-0621-taking-account-of-carbon-reduction-plans-in-the-procurement-of-major-government-contracts/guidance-on-adopting-and-applying-ppn-0621-selection-criteria-html?utm_source=chatgpt.com][_GOV.UK Assets+1GOV.UK+1_|https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67b33f6b4e79a175a4c2fd80/PPN_006_Taking_account_of_Carbon_Reduction_Plans.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com]

_This approach ensures that the CRP remains relevant and accurately reflects the emissions associated with the contract's delivery.​_

_It's important to note that this provision is intended as a temporary measure. Bidding entities are expected to develop and publish their own CRPs as soon as reasonably practicable.​_[_GOV.UK Assets_|https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67b33f6b4e79a175a4c2fd80/PPN_006_Taking_account_of_Carbon_Reduction_Plans.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com]

Please note however that *Bolt Ops UK is not wholly owned by Bolt Operations OU -* it is ultimately owned by Bolt Technology OU. 

That said, I would rather err on the side of caution and go with the intent and spirit of the policy and include Bolt Operations OU data (the actual operational group entity) even if it is not the bidder or the parent entity. 

This avoids presenting an artificially low emissions footprint (greenwashing).

[~accountid:6390a8e6f48fbd9b62d9ca77] I see in the excel file that you used *Currency Rates as of Date* report.
This is WD build-in report, that takes the date-time you put into prompt as local time, converts it into UTC and then gives you the rate based on on the information according to UTC.
Example: 

* you in Tallinn put into prompt “31.03.2025 00:00” - now we have summer time +03 hours to UTC, so WD will provide the rate effective on 30.03.2025 21:00
* you in Tallinn put into prompt “01.04.2025 00:00” - WD will provide the rate effective on 31.03.2025 21:00
* {color:#403294}correct case{color} - you in Tallinn should put into prompt “{color:#403294}01.04.2025 03:00{color}” - WD will provide the rate effective on 01.04.2025 00:00 = 31.03.2025 24:00

_Started form January 2025 all our currency rates in WD uploaded with the timestamp 23:59:59 UTC (which is shown as 00:00 next day)_

* 3.2 - please consider if we can provide daily reports.

* 4.4 - we should not take responsibility for the acts of third parties (couriers). Suggested change reduces our reclassification risks. Importance: {color:#ff5630}*high*{color}.
* 4.5 - just FYI.
* 5.4.1 and Exhibit C - due to reclassification risk we should not commit to service levels related to delivery. Why would I go for the amendment instead of a new agreement?

* The original agreement already allows for renewal and amendments, so there’s no legal need for a new contract.
* It ensures continuity of terms and avoids the risk of introducing inconsistencies or renegotiating existing clauses.
* It provides a clear audit trail, keeping the agreement history in one place.

During our meeting, we discussed the wider question of who should decide which team can access a resource. The most logical answer brought up was that it should be the owner of the resource. This topic affects the implementation details of this ticket.

After the meeting we had some options on the table. This is not a definitive list, just what we have come up with at the current moment.

h2. Option 1: One Policy per Team + One Access Application per Directory

Currently we have all of the access applications configured in a single file. This doesn’t give us much access control and later down the line, the Terraform plan and apply operations will slow down, since there is so much state to work with. This is a problem that we are already experiencing with the {{bolt.eu}} and {{taxify.eu}} Route53 records already - plan takes something like 5 minutes or more if I recall correctly.

Instead of this, we could structure it to have a separate directory for each access application. This would allow us to set the engineering team (basically anyone with GitHub access) that owns the application as a CODEOWNER in that directory. This would offload some work away from our side and also grant some actual access control, since the owner of a service has more knowledge of who should be accessing an application than anyone from our team.

One of the concerns is that the CODEOWNERS file could get much longer because of this. Not sure how big of an issue this actually is, since the one on {{bolt-server}} is also over 2700 lines long. This seems to pretty usual for monorepos. There are some tools that allow breaking up long CODEOWNERS files, [such as this one|https://github.com/andrewring/github-distributed-owners], however I would consider this topic outside of this task’s scope.

The other concern is that on Thursday, we decided to write the Terraform code to automatically create access policies when they are referenced in an access application. If we split up the access policies to separate states, then this can’t be implemented in a sensible manner - theoretically we might be able to use a {{data}} block to lookup if the policy exists and create it if it doesn’t but this would create a situation where all of the policies would exist in different state directories seemingly randomly. If we were to attempt to delete an access application, then we could also be attempting to delete some policies that were created alongside with it. At that point these policies could already be in use by other access applications as well. A very messy setup and I think we should definitely avoid this path.

I think that if we were to go with this solution, then access policies should be created by an Okta workflow using the CloudFlare API instead.

h2. Option 2: One Policy per Access Application + IT Team Manages Policies

This approach is completely different and offloads the access management to IT. With this approach we wouldn’t have an easy way to see a list of applications that a team can access however.

Another concern is the permissions - can we restrict IT to only manage access application? In other words, is the CloudFlare access control granular enough? To me, it seems like we can only grant full access to Zero Trust, not for edit access to any specific ZT resource.

Also, just in case confirming over [~accountid:712020:0f7a089b-3b06-423b-844c-6e5ac370aa1e]  that you understand how the tier pricing applies. According to the current wording if there are tiered discounts for seats , the discount only applies to the seats that fall within each specific tier, not to all seats.

h4. Example:

Let’s say the pricing tiers are like this:

* *1–50 seats*: No discount
* *51–100 seats*: 10% discount
* *101+ seats*: 20% discount

If you buy *120 seats*, here's how it works:

* First 50 seats = full price (no discount)
* Next 50 seats (51–100) = 10% discount
* Last 20 seats (101–120) = 20% discount

So the discounts *only apply* to the seats *within each tier range*, not to all 120 seats.

If you reduce the number of seats you're using, the *seats with the biggest discounts are removed first*.

h4. Using the same example:

If you reduce your seat count from 120 to 100:

* The *20 seats removed* will come from the *101–120 range* — which had the *20% discount*
* You’ll lose the *highest discounted seats first*, so now you’re only getting the 10% discount for seats 51–100

Hi [@anna.aalberg|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U02EVPGJ9NZ]! As with many legal questions, there’s no black-and-white answer, it really comes down to how you frame the argument 🙂 

Article 22 of the Directive says we can’t “pre-tick” any _additional payments_ on top of the our _main contractual obligation_*_._* I’d argue that delivery is part of our _core service,_ not an optional extra, and therefore not an “additional payment” under Article 22.
This [commission|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021XC1229%2804%29&qid=1745253964962] notice gives examples of what _would_ count as additional services, e.g.  “express delivery” or a “maintenance contract” when buying electronics, or travel insurance with a flight. Those are clearly add-ons.
In contrast, our delivery functionality is *an integral part of the platform.*  This is reflected in our TCs (even in the title: “General Terms to Bolt Food *_delivery_* service with the Client”). So I’d say the spirit of the directive is aimed at avoiding hidden or optional costs, not core elements of a bundled service like ours. (edited) 

But in any case, unless there has been any consumer authority inquiries based on this, I don’t think this is anything to worry about for now 🙂 It’s not a black and white situation and we are not going to make any changes to the product just to be safe, as the change would negatively effect the user experience (as the majority of orders are delivery orders and this would add another “click” in the user flow)

It’s quite difficult to tell which payments the customer is referring to as there are no payment details and the transactions have been converted from UAH to EUR. 
However, after converting the amounts to EUR it seems the charges are related to these 2 payments. Both of these payments had an adjustment. Authorization adjustments can cause multiple movements on the customers bank account. I can confirm that everything looks fine from Bolt’s end. 
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3254039804|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3254039804]
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3254091006|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3254091006]

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount. 


Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Cheers,
Marten

Hi [~accountid:712020:9c263122-6bc1-4bbe-91d7-c80d616c4514] , thanks so much for the clear context! 🙏 

* *Regarding data collection,* I think that the easiest way would be to split our and CarScan responsibilities, where CarScan would be taking care of their end (information validation and information obligation, where they could give us a confirmation in the agreement that they confirm that data is valid + that they’ve informed the data subjects). I think we can advise CarScan to collect authorizations/prep notices, but if we “drive” this initiative ourselves, we’ll bear the responsibility for it, and it’ll be complex from an operational POV. So, in short, I’d say let’s add this to the contract + ask CarScan to ensure that the data is transferred lawfully and that data is valid.
* *Regarding the database and informing the data subjects*, I think it’s a very operational question. Has the local ops team commented on whether they’d be able to / willing to reach out to the drivers via email/other means to inform them about this? If not, do we want to inform the data subjects via Privacy Notices? If that’s not doable, then we perhaps can ask CarScan to include this information in their comms, and inform the data subjects this way. Generally, we’ve had similar (though not identical) initiatives in EU countries. There, we decided to take one of the following approaches: (1) inform users via email - as we don’t offer detailed/tailored privacy notices per-country, we asked Local Ops to send email comms to the drivers; (2) rely on the Privacy Notice - where the activity potentially falls under a data processing activity we already describe in the notice, even vaguely, and when the activity is low-risk due to low amount of data and low amount of data subjects, we opted for this option, (3) we asked the partner to inform the users in their comms (and, for example, to add a link to our Privacy Notice to inform the users about further use of data and user rights), as they have a closer connection to the users, they have their contact details, which we might not have.



Happy to discuss this further - let me know what you think!

The limitation is from MBWay, they can only process one refund per transaction (full or partial refund). The choice to make it a full or partial refund depends on the user’s demand and the type of refund they qualify to according to CS rules.

The partial refund is not a concept created and used only by Bolt. It exists with other merchants but we recently implemented it to be able to refund users to their payment methods. Previously, partial refunds for Bolt orders were only made to Bolt balance. But now it can be done to most of the payment methods used by customers on the Bolt platform.

Hi [~accountid:603fcbd5333ff40070e0e343] 

While our Passenger Terms and Conditions (*clause 17(c)*, see screenshot) clearly state that passengers are responsible for their own belongings, this situation is a bit different.

Here, the passenger believed the driver stole their phone - which wasn’t the case. The driver did the right thing and reported the lost phone. The issue came from our side, as the agent didn’t check NotLost before the item was given away. So, the phone was effectively mishandled by us. Because of that, there’s a risk that if the passenger becomes aware of what happened, they could claim Bolt was negligent (although in my view, the likelihood of this materialising is low, as the passenger does not currently appear to be aware of the internal error). I understand [~accountid:614ad8fe76e34d006967d6bd] has checked this with the Public Policy team and they have not raised any regulatory red flags, therefore, this is ultimately a business decision rather than a legal one.

To avoid further back-and-forth with the passenger (especially as this has been dragging on since last year), my recommendation is to offer the full value of the phone as a one-off goodwill gesture. That way, we close the loop without adding more frustration on their end. My advice would be to ensure the amount offered reasonably covers the cost of a replacement phone (I would not offer less than the value of the passengers phone). 

When communicating this to the passenger, frame it clearly as a one-time goodwill gesture - and avoid any wording that could be read as Bolt admitting fault.

Let me know if you have any questions.

Thanks

High-level privacy analysis, prepared to be consistent for the one used for Delivery vertical.

h3. What’s good:

* *Sampling rate (0.01%)* is privacy-friendly, minimizing the amount of data subjects concerned.
* *No cookies involved*, Mixpanel SDK uses device IDs (which are pseudonymous).
* *Option to mask screens/fields* exists - essential for data minimisation; needs clarification on what can be masked.
* *No special category data involved*, assuming masking of sensitive screens (selfie check, payment, profile, etc.) is applied consistently.

h3. Key privacy considerations:

# *Data minimisation*
→ Confirm that masking is active for:
#* Screens with direct identifiers (e.g. name, phone, card info)
#* Any input fields or personal details (e.g. delivery address, ID verification)
# *Purpose limitation*
→ Primary purpose = improve UX, not profiling or automated decision-making
→ Ensure this is reflected in internal docs + privacy notices (if not yet done)
# *Legal basis*
→ Legitimate interest is OK _if_ masking and low sampling are enforced
→ Will log an LIA 
# *Retention*
→ Ideally, follow Bolt Market’s 30-day rule for session replays (unless there’s a strong reason to keep longer)

h3. ⚠️ Additional to clarify:

* Will recordings ever be linked back to user profiles or internal order data?
* Are we planning to use these replays in future ML/AI training?

May I interfere? I understand that we want to call drivers as soon as possible so the suspension is as short as possible, but I have few points on this.

If the driver is waiting orders, we can of course call them as they have time at that moment.

If the driver has an active order, and we call them to discuss safety-related matter, they will either:


* Answer the phone and tell us to call later (it might be even an hour because the trip could be long).
** In this case it makes more sense to me just to put the suspension as they will notice immediately they are suspended after they finish order and reach out to us. We also always open a conversation stating what they were accused for and that we need their explanation and tell them also to reach out to us once they finish the order.

* Answer the phone and continue to communicate the situation.
** In this case it might be a really unpleasant experience for the rider, e.g.:
*** Driver holding phone and calling
*** Driver using hands free but calling during the ride
*** Driver talking on the phone and discussing uncomfortable topics, such as:
**** Being intoxicated
**** Groping another rider
**** Stealing from another rider



Anyway, in both cases it seems that the process is rather problematic and the issue could be resolved just by not calling them during active order but rather in calling hours + waiting order.



What are your thoughts on this?



Thank you for your answer.
